params.question: In the opening scenario, the child with stridor and cyanosis is triaged before the adult with facial trauma and gurgling. Both have airway compromise. What clinical finding makes the child's situation more immediately life-threatening?

answers.text: Stridor always indicates complete airway obstruction requiring immediate surgical intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stridor indicates turbulent airflow through a partially obstructed airway, not complete obstruction. The critical finding here is cyanosis, which signals that tissue oxygenation has failed.

answers.text: Cyanosis indicates active tissue hypoxia with imminent cardiac arrest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cyanosis means oxygen delivery has fallen below the threshold for tissue survival. Cardiac arrest follows within minutes, making this child the most time-critical patient under the ABCDE framework.

answers.text: A child's airway is anatomically narrower, so any foreign body causes total obstruction instantly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While paediatric airways are narrower, the triage priority is based on clinical signs of hypoxia, not anatomy alone. The adult also has airway compromise; what differentiates them is the cyanosis indicating active oxygen failure.

answers.text: Foreign body aspiration is inherently more dangerous than traumatic airway injuries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both mechanisms can be equally lethal. Triage priority is determined by clinical signs — consciousness, colour, and respiratory effort — not by the cause of the obstruction.

overallFeedback.feedback: Cyanosis is the key differentiator. It signals that tissue oxygenation has failed and cardiac arrest is imminent. The ABCDE framework prioritises the most immediately life-threatening presentation based on clinical signs, not mechanism of injury.

Correct! Cyanosis signals active hypoxia with imminent cardiac arrest. Under the ABCDE framework, this makes the child the highest priority, ahead of the adult whose airway is compromised but still partially maintained.

interactions.label: A 4-year-old child has a button battery lodged in the left nostril. The object i

params.question: A 4-year-old child has a button battery lodged in the left nostril. The object is not clearly visible on anterior rhinoscopy. What is the correct course of action?

answers.text: Refer for removal under general anaesthesia, as the standard rule requires visualisation before attempting extraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the correct approach for inert foreign bodies, but button batteries are the explicit exception. Chemical and electrical necrosis begins within 1–2 hours and cannot wait for an elective theatre slot.

answers.text: Apply a topical decongestant to reduce mucosal swelling and improve visualisation before attempting removal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Applying a decongestant wastes critical time. Button battery injury is time-dependent — every minute of mucosal contact worsens the chemical and electrical burn.

answers.text: Remove immediately, as button battery necrosis begins within 1–2 hours and overrides the standard referral rule

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A button battery generates an electrical current and leaks alkali, causing full-thickness mucosal necrosis within 1–2 hours. This is the one scenario where immediate removal overrides the general rule of referring unseen foreign bodies.

answers.text: Instil olive oil to insulate the battery from the mucosa while arranging elective removal the next morning

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Olive oil does not neutralise the electrochemical injury from a button battery. Any delay risks septal perforation, and elective scheduling is inappropriate for this emergency.

overallFeedback.feedback: For inert foreign bodies, you stop and refer if you cannot visualise the object. But button batteries are the explicit exception — alkaline leakage and electrical current cause mucosal necrosis within 1–2 hours, so immediate removal is mandatory.

Correct! Button batteries are the one exception to the 'stop and refer if unseen' rule. Electrical and chemical necrosis begins within 1–2 hours, so immediate removal is mandatory regardless of site or visualisation.

interactions.label: A 35-year-old woman with chronic suppurative otitis media and a known central pe

params.question: A 35-year-old woman with chronic suppurative otitis media and a known central perforation of the tympanic membrane presents with otorrhoea. Which prescription and technique is appropriate?

answers.text: Neomycin–dexamethasone drops instilled with the affected ear facing up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neomycin is an aminoglycoside. With a perforated tympanic membrane, it passes through to the round window and can damage the cochlea, causing iatrogenic sensorineural hearing loss.

answers.text: Ciprofloxacin drops warmed in the palms, instilled with the affected ear up, followed by tragal pumping

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ciprofloxacin is a quinolone — safe with perforation as it is not ototoxic at topical concentrations. Warming prevents caloric dizziness, and tragal pumping drives drops deeper into the canal.

answers.text: Gentamicin drops applied after pulling the pinna downward and backward

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Two errors: gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, contraindicated with perforation due to cochlear toxicity. Also, in adults the pinna is pulled upward and backward to straighten the canal; downward and backward is for young children.

answers.text: Ciprofloxacin drops taken directly from the refrigerator, instilled with the affected ear facing down

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cold drops trigger caloric vertigo, causing the patient to stop using them. The affected ear must face upward so the drops enter and remain in the canal rather than draining out immediately.

overallFeedback.feedback: Two principles apply together: first, only quinolone drops (not aminoglycosides like neomycin or gentamicin) are safe when the tympanic membrane is perforated. Second, warm the drops, position the affected ear up, pull the adult pinna upward and backward, and use tragal pumping.

Correct! With a perforated tympanic membrane, only quinolone drops (such as ciprofloxacin) are safe. Warm the bottle, position the affected ear up, instil without touching the skin, and use tragal pumping to drive drops deeper.

interactions.label: While consenting a patient for mastoidectomy, you state: 'There is a very small

params.question: While consenting a patient for mastoidectomy, you state: 'There is a very small risk of facial nerve injury.' The patient appears satisfied. What is the most critical element missing from your disclosure?

answers.text: The exact percentage of facial nerve injury from published surgical audits

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A percentage alone is still incomplete. The patient needs to understand what the injury would mean for them functionally, not just the statistical odds.

answers.text: The specific consequence: inability to close the eye and drooping of the mouth corner

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Stating a risk without naming its consequence is the most dangerous consent error. The patient must understand that facial nerve injury means difficulty closing the eye, mouth asymmetry, and potential need for further corrective surgery.

answers.text: The name and experience level of the operating surgeon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While relevant to general consent, this is not the critical missing element in risk disclosure. The core deficiency is failing to describe what facial nerve injury would mean for the patient's daily life.

answers.text: A written comparison of complication rates between mastoidectomy and conservative management

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Comparative statistics are not a standard component of risk disclosure. The fundamental requirement is that every named risk is paired with its functional consequence for the patient.

overallFeedback.feedback: Frequency alone is not enough. Saying 'very small risk' without naming what it means for the patient is the most dangerous consent error. Facial nerve injury means difficulty closing the eye and drooping of the mouth corner — the patient must hear both the odds and the outcome.

Correct! 'Very small risk' without naming the consequence is the most dangerous consent error. Always pair the frequency with what the patient would experience — facial nerve injury means inability to close the eye and asymmetry of the mouth.

interactions.label: At a factory screening camp, a 42-year-old worker's audiogram shows a dip at 4 k

params.question: At a factory screening camp, a 42-year-old worker's audiogram shows a dip at 4 kHz with normal thresholds at other frequencies. His otoacoustic emissions are abnormal. What is the most appropriate action?

answers.text: Reassure the worker that an isolated frequency dip is a normal variant and schedule routine annual review

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A 4 kHz notch in a noise-exposed worker is NOT a normal variant. It is the earliest sign of noise-induced hearing loss and a key marker for occupational compensation. Reassurance is inappropriate.

answers.text: Recommend hearing protection and refer for auditory brainstem response testing to confirm the diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The 4 kHz notch requires immediate protective measures. An abnormal OAE does not confirm hearing loss — it calls for a repeat test or ABR referral. Protection must begin now while diagnosis is being confirmed.

answers.text: Diagnose noise-induced sensorineural hearing loss and immediately fit a hearing aid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A hearing aid is premature. An abnormal OAE alone does not confirm hearing loss — ABR is needed for diagnostic confirmation. A 4 kHz notch with preserved other frequencies does not yet indicate hearing-aid-level impairment.

answers.text: Advise the worker to change occupation immediately, as noise-induced hearing loss always progresses to profound deafness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While noise-induced hearing loss is irreversible, it does not always progress to profound deafness. With adequate hearing protection and exposure kept below 85 dB, further damage can be prevented without necessarily changing occupation.

overallFeedback.feedback: A worker with a 4 kHz notch needs protection and follow-up, not reassurance. An abnormal OAE does not confirm hearing loss — it calls for a repeat test or ABR referral. The 4 kHz notch is the earliest sign and a medicolegal marker for occupational compensation.

Correct! The 4 kHz notch is the earliest audiometric marker of noise-induced hearing loss. An abnormal OAE warrants ABR referral for confirmation, not immediate diagnosis. Hearing protection must begin right away.
